content_list.content_text: Latin America is a vast and diverse region. Geographically, it covers all the territory stretching from the southern tip of South America to the California border and the Caribbean islands. Politically, in the 1960s it was home to both Brazil's right-wing military government and Cuban communism. In cinema, some of its countries built major industries before and during the 1960s, while others had minimal film production.

information.contentText: Despite the simple story, director Glauber Rocha tells it allegorically, mixing cordel literature and opera, and giving priority to the music and folk rituals of the people of Brazil's Northeast. Glauber wraps the narrative in the metalinguistic gaze common to Cinema Novo. The dragging camera and the vibrant Northeastern music give almost the impression of a continuation of Black God, White Devil. Many consider it the masterpiece of Master Glauber, blending the Northeastern anthropophagic ritual, its "sect," and its folklore in an apotheotic encounter with a different way of making films, following the parameters of Cinema Novo - by then past the experimental phase of the first wave of films.

content_list.content_text: The most important national cinema in South America was probably Brazil's. Significant works appeared in Brazilian cinema in the 1930s, but its great leap came in the early 1960s with the flourishing Cinema Novo, a movement whose motto was "an idea in the head and a camera in the hand".

The most prominent figure of Cinema Novo was writer-director Glauber Rocha (1939-1981), whose best-known film, Antonio das Mortes (1969), is the story of a gunman hired to kill bandits who ends up becoming a revolutionary.

content_list.title: One of the films that changed the history of Brazilian cinema
content_list.description:
Upon attending one of the first screenings of Black God, White Devil, a Brazilian critic reportedly exclaimed: "My God, Eisenstein has been reborn... and he's Brazilian!" Born in Bahia, a Brazilian state known as the cradle of Afro-Brazilian culture, Glauber grew up fascinated by mysticism and American Westerns. In his early twenties, he moved to Rio de Janeiro, where he fell in with a group of young cinephiles who would go on to found the influential Cinema Novo movement.

Influenced by radical politics like so many of his generation, Glauber sought to explore the links between historical change and violence in Black God, White Devil. Here he focuses on examples of popular uprisings in the Brazilian backlands.

Shot in an arid black and white that makes the screen practically shimmer with heat, Black God, White Devil alternates frenetic camera movements with dynamically edited sequences, layering Villa-Lobos's music over wind, screams, and gunshots. The final effect is a sense that the film and the country it portrays are about to explode. Shortly before the film was completed and released commercially, the Brazilian military staged a coup, ushering in a dictatorship that lasted 20 years.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Richard Peña, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: Influenced by Italian Neorealism and the French New Wave, Glauber made his film debut in 1962 with The Turning Wind (1962) and then directed Black God, White Devil (1964), an extraordinary visual study of life in the backlands that combines local legend with music by J. S. Bach and Heitor Villa-Lobos to deliver a harsh critique of survival conditions in the drought-stricken, impoverished Northeast. The 1964 military coup imposed growing difficulties on the Brazilian film industry, to which Glauber responded with the allegorical Entranced Earth (1967).

In contrast to the stylization of Glauber Rocha's films, other Cinema Novo figures opted for a more realistic style. Former documentary director Nelson Pereira dos Santos (b. 1928) made Barren Lives (1963), a harsh account of rural poverty in the desolate landscape of the Northeast. Ruy Guerra (b. 1931) made The Guns (1964), a vigorous study of a group of soldiers tasked with protecting a warehouse from starving peasants.

movies.title: Aruanda
movies.overview: A história de formação do quilombo Olho d'Água na Serra do Talhado em Santa Lúcia do Sabugi, alto sertão da Paraíba. A fundação feita pelo ex-escravo Zé Bento e sua família que sobreviveu cultivando algodão e produzindo cerâmica nos períodos de grande estiagem. A comunidade no início dos anos 1960 e o isolamento permanente do resto do Brasil.

movies.title: Arraial do Cabo
movies.overview: Com fotografia deslumbrante de Mário Carneiro, que codirige o filme, e texto do jornalista Claudio Mello Souza, o documentário mostra as transformações sociais e as interferências nas formas primitivas de vida de pescadores do vilarejo de Arraial do Cabo, no litoral do Estado do Rio de Janeiro. A Fábrica Nacional de Álcalis, que se instalou no local, causa a morte dos peixes, o que faz com que muitos integrantes da comunidade partam em busca de trabalho. Os modos tradicionais de produção se chocam com os problemas da industrialização. Gravuras de Oswaldo Goeldi abrem o filme. (Cinemateca Brasileira)

movies.title: Cinco Vezes Favela
movies.overview: Cinco histórias de moradores de favela. 1- "Um Favelado": Um favelado, desempregado e sem dinheiro, arquiteta um plano para ganhar dinheiro, mas é descoberto e preso pela polícia.  2- "Zé da Cachorra": Um latifundiário quer de volta suas terras, onde está instalada uma favela. Um favelado luta contra a passividade de uma comissão de moradores, que estão aceitando a situação desfavorável que lhes foi imposta.  3- "Escola de Samba Alegria de Viver": Um favelado, presidente do grêmio recreativo, divide-se entre lutar pela sua categoria ou aceitar as imposições comerciais do carnaval.  4- "Couro de Gato": Moradores favelados caçam gatos a fim de usar seu couro para fabricar tamborins, que serão usados no carnaval.  5- "Pedreira de São Diogo": No Rio de Janeiro, sobre uma pedreira há uma favela. Ao perceberem o risco de desabamento dos barracos, em consequência das explosões de dinamite, os operários incitam os moradores a iniciar movimento de resistência para impedir um acidente fatal.

movies.title: Barravento
movies.overview: Numa aldeia de pescadores de xeréu, cujos antepassados vieram da África como escravos, permanecem antigos cultos místicos ligados ao candomblé. Firmino é um antigo morador, que foi para Salvador na tentativa de escapar da pobreza. Ao retornar ele sente atração por Cota, ao mesmo tempo em que não consegue esquecer sua antiga paixão, Naína, que, por sua vez, gosta de Aruã. Firmino encomenda um despacho contra Aruã, que não é atingido. O alvo termina sendo a própria aldeia, que passa a ser impedida de pescar.

movies.title: Os Cafajestes
movies.overview: Jandir (Jece Valadão) e seu amigo Vavá (Daniel Filho), um playboy, vivem no mundo das drogas e sexo de Copacabana. Só que a situação de Vavá não é boa, já que seu pai corre o risco de perder tudo o que tem. É quando a dupla tem a ideia de tirar fotos comprometedoras de Leda (Norma Bengell), a amante do tio de Vavá, no intuito de chantageá-lo. Eles a levam a uma praia deserta e, após tirarem as fotos, a estupram.

movies.title: Ganga Zumba
movies.overview: No Nordeste brasileiro, entre os séculos 16 e 17, alguns escravos de um engenho de cana-de-açúcar tramam uma fuga para o Quilombo dos Palmares, uma comunidade de negros fugidos da escravidão, na Serra da Barriga. Entre eles, encontra-se o jovem Ganga Zumba (Antonio Pitanga), futuro líder daquela república revolucionária, a primeira de toda a América.

movies.title: Vidas Secas
movies.overview: Uma família miserável tenta escapar da seca no sertão nordestino. Fabiano (Átila Iório), Sinhá Vitória (Maria Ribeiro), seus dois filhos e a cachorra Baleia vagam sem destino e já quase sem esperanças pelos confins do interior, sobrevivendo às forças da natureza e à crueldade dos homens. Adaptação da obra de Graciliano Ramos.

movies.original_title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol
movies.title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol
movies.overview: Manuel vive com a esposa Rosa e a mãe, numa vida muito pobre no sertão brasileiro. Numa discussão com o Coronel que controla sua região o rapaz se revolta e mata o poderoso. Sua única opção é fugir deixando o pouco que tem para trás e seguindo o beato Sebastião que promete a bênção de Deus aos seus fiéis. Manuel pode, sem querer, estar novamente entrando em problemas, pois a oligarquia local encomendou a morte de Sebastião e seus seguidores a João das Mortes, com medo que uma situação como a de Canudos se repita.

movies.title: Os Fuzis
movies.overview: Um grupo de soldados armados é enviado para o Nordeste do Brasil na tentativa de impedir que uma população atingida pela fome invada e roube um depósito de alimentos no sertão agreste. Enquanto a alienação e a insanidade das pessoas levadas à alucinação por sua fome latente é conduzida pelas previsões de uma figura religiosa, um motorista de caminhão observa a situação e permanece dividido entre sua amizade com os soldados e sua revolta contra a falta de ação do governo na luta contra a miséria que persiste na região.

movies.title: O Desafio
movies.overview: Passivamente enfrentando a repressão imposta pela ditadura militar no Brasil nos anos 60, um jornalista entra em uma crise pessoal, agravada por seu caso de amor com a esposa de um industrial, que não quer sair de sua casa por causa do filho.

movies.title: Terra em Transe
movies.overview: O jornalista e poeta Paulo Martins oscila entre diversas forças políticas que lutam pelo poder no fictício país de Eldorado: D. Porfírio Diaz, um líder de direita e político de tradição, D. Felipe Vieira, governador da Província de Alecrim, líder populista e demagógico, e D. Julio Fuentes, poderoso empresário dono de um império de comunicação. Numa conversa com a militante Sara, Paulo conclui que o povo de Eldorado precisa de um líder e que Vieira possui tais atributos. Eldorado encontra-se entre o golpe de estado e o populismo, entre a crise e a transformação. E Paulo, dividido entre a poesia e a política, agoniza sem conseguir solucionar as incoerências de Eldorado e as suas próprias contradições.

movies.title: O Bravo Guerreiro
movies.overview: Miguel Horta, jovem deputado da oposição, decide mudar de partido para se infiltrar no governo por julgar que só dentro do poder é que poderia fazer alguma coisa pela causa pública. Um dia recebe em casa a visita de um cabo eleitoral dizendo que pelegos estão tentando derrubar a diretoria do sindicato, tendo por motivo um projeto de lei de sua autoria. Apesar dos apelos de Clara, sua mulher, Miguel vai para o sindicato, onde os trabalhadores estão reunidos em assembleia geral. Quando o presidente do sindicato consegue superar a situação, Miguel faz um discurso narrando toda a sua trajetória política e termina dizendo que não é mais o indicado para defender os sindicalizados. De volta ao lar, percorrendo a casa vazia, vai até a escrivaninha, pega um revólver e encosta o cano no céu da boca." (Guia de Filmes, 21) (Cinemateca Brasileira)

movies.title: Fome de Amor
movies.overview: Alfredo, ex-revolucionário, cego, surdo e mudo, e sua mulher recebem, numa casa de veraneio, uma pianista frustrada e seu marido. A troca de casais se estabelece para que, ao final, a dissociação se imponha como um gesto de libertação.

movies.original_title: O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro
movies.title: O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro
movies.overview: Continuação de Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol. Misturando cordel e ópera, esta aventura apresenta o personagem Antônio das Mortes, que recebe a tarefa de eliminar um novo cangaceiro da região. No caminho, ele encontra diversos jagunços e coroneis e se vê cara a cara com o povo do sertão e com as dificuldades enfrentadas pelos sertanejos, eventos que farão Antonio adquirir uma nova perspectiva de vida.

movies.title: Macunaíma
movies.overview: Macunaíma é um herói preguiçoso, safado e sem nenhum caráter. Ele nasceu na selva e de preto, virou branco. Depois de adulto, deixa o sertão em companhia dos irmãos. Macunaíma vive várias aventuras na cidade, conhecendo e amando guerrilheiras e prostitutas, enfrentando vilões milionários, policiais, personagens de todos os tipos.

movies.title: Os Herdeiros
movies.overview: Para ganhar um neto, o decadente Barão do Café Joaquim resolve casar a filha com Jorge, um repórter da capital. Anos depois, Jorge trai o sogro, foge com a mulher e deixa o filho na fazenda.

movies.original_title: Como Era Gostoso o Meu Francês
movies.title: Como Era Gostoso o Meu Francês
movies.overview: No Brasil de 1594, um aventureiro francês prisioneiro dos Tupinambás escapa da morte graças aos seus conhecimentos de artilharia. Segundo a cultura Tupinambás, é preciso devorar o inimigo para adquirir todos os seus poderes, no caso saber utilizar a pólvora e os canhões. Enquanto aguarda ser executado, o francês aprende os hábitos dos Tupinambás e se une a uma índia e através dela toma conhecimento de um tesouro enterrado e decide fugir. A índia se recusa a segui-lo e após a batalha com a tribo inimiga, o chefe Cunhambebe marca a data da execução: o ritual antropofágico será parte das comemorações pela vitória.

movies.title: Pindorama
movies.overview: Ambientado durante o período da descoberta e colonização inicial do Brasil. O título refere-se a uma palavra que os povos nativos usavam para as terras costeiras: "pindorama" ou "lugar das pequenas árvores". Um filme pesado e grandioso, foi vaiado quando foi exibido no Festival de Cannes de 1971.

information.contentTitle: Key Films of Cinema Novo in Brazil
information.contentText: The main releases that defined the Cinema Novo movement in Brazil.

content_list.content_text: Toward the end of the decade, after the successive coups of 1964 and 1968, Joaquim Pedro de Andrade (1932-1988) made Macunaima (1969), a wild comedy on racial, sexual, and political themes adapted from Mário de Andrade's novel of the same name.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Black God, White Devil
information.contentText: Shot in 1963 in Monte Santo, the region where Antônio Conselheiro lived and preached, "Black God, White Devil" opened to the public three months after the coup. Its striking direction and its theme of conflict over land - at a time when the Peasant Leagues had already been banned - made an impact. The film was acclaimed at the Cannes Film Festival. It would later be banned by the censors.

content_list.content_text: The 1960s also brought Brazilian cinema its most important international award. The Given Word (1962), by Anselmo Duarte (1920-2009) - the story of a small landowner who vows to carry a cross to a distant church if his sick donkey recovers - won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival, and remains to this day the only Brazilian winner of the prestigious prize.

Duarte explored similar religious themes with The Obsessed of Catulé (1964), a film about a man who believes he is Jesus Christ. The socially critical aspects of these works led to Anselmo Duarte being arrested as a suspected communist. He was also criticized by the Cinema Novo filmmakers.

information.contentText: Based on the play of the same name by playwright Dias Gomes, it remains to this day the only Brazilian film to win the Palme d'Or, the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival in France, one of the most prestigious and famous film festivals in the world. Brazil and the United States are the only countries in the Americas to have won the honor. The Given Word also became the first South American film to be nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, at the 1963 ceremony, but the winner was the French film Les dimanches de Ville d'Avray.

content_list.content_text: A movement parallel to Brazil's Cinema Novo developed in Mexico, where a group of young critics created the magazine Nuevo Cine and leveled harsh criticism at Mexican commercial cinema and its reliance on safe genres such as musicals and comedies.

content_list.title: Cinema Novo: Main Characteristics
content_list.description:
In his 1965 text The Aesthetics of Hunger, Glauber Rocha wrote: "We know - we who made these ugly, sad films, these screaming, desperate films in which reason did not always prevail - that hunger will not be cured by bureaucratic planning and that Technicolor patches do not hide, but rather aggravate, its tumors. Thus, only a culture of hunger, undermining its own structures, can surpass itself qualitatively: and the noblest cultural manifestation of hunger is violence."

As the movement's main aesthetic features, lack of resources and creative freedom allowed Cinema Novo filmmakers to challenge, provoke, and surprise audiences. However, this freedom, this abandonment of technical preciousness, made each film an expression of its director's personal vision. For this reason, the movement is not necessarily homogeneous in its aesthetics, since the form and content of the films varied greatly across its different phases.

Cinema Novo was shaped in the image of other movements known for their subversiveness, such as Italian Neorealism and the French New Wave. Like their predecessors, the Brazilians wanted to shoot on small budgets, often on real locations and with nonprofessional actors, addressing themes drawn from the reality of the oppressed classes. A passion for cinema and the desire to use it as a tool for change was what drove them all.

Although some Cinema Novo directors saw the French as bourgeois or elitist, they agreed that the "auteur theory" of the French New Wave was an interesting concept that allowed filmmakers to imprint their personal views on their works, including political opinions and aesthetic preferences.

For this reason, the movement has no aesthetic unity. The "aesthetics of hunger" itself, developed by Glauber Rocha, dealt more with conceptual issues than with visual or technical ones. The goal was to expose social inequality in Third World countries and to speak of hunger as a symptom of a sick society. As the filmmaker put it: "[…] our greatest misery is that this hunger, though felt, is not understood."
content_list.credits: Summary based on the articles "Cinema Novo" by Katia Kreutz on aicinema.com

content_list.content_text: J. M. García Ascot (1927-1986), a member of the Nuevo Cine circle, suggested alternative paths for Mexican cinema in En el balcón vacío (On the Empty Balcony, 1961), based on his wife's childhood memories of the Spanish Civil War and her exile in Mexico, described by John King as "a Proustian evocation of lost time".

In 1965 and 1966, two important film adaptations of stories by Colombian writer Gabriel García Márquez were made: There Are No Thieves in This Village (1965), by Alberto Isaac (1925-1988), and Tiempo de morir (Time to Die, 1966), by Arturo Ripstein (b. 1943).

The most illustrious film artist working in Mexico, however, was the Spanish émigré Luis Buñuel (1900-1983), who had left his home country at the time of the Civil War. Buñuel built a remarkable career in the Mexican industry throughout the 1950s with films such as Los olvidados (The Young and the Damned, 1950), Él (This Strange Passion, 1953), and Nazarín (1958), blends of social commentary and surrealism.

information.contentText: Memories of Underdevelopment is a 1968 fiction film shot in Havana by director and screenwriter Tomás Gutiérrez Alea. The film examines the situation in Cuba right after its socialist revolution through the eyes of Sergio, a 38-year-old petit-bourgeois Cuban who decides to stay in the country after his family flees to the United States.

content_list.content_text: Among Buñuel's last Mexican films is El ángel exterminador (The Exterminating Angel, 1962), a chilling parable about a group of people trapped at a dinner party that - inexplicably - no one can leave. This account of the discreet charm of the bourgeoisie set the tone for the last 15 years of Buñuel's career, but, with the exception of the satirical Simón del desierto (Simon of the Desert, 1965), all his subsequent films would be made in Europe.

Apart from Brazil's and Mexico's, the most notable film industry in Latin America was Argentina's. Leopoldo Torre Nilsson (1924-1978) had already won international acclaim in the late 1950s for his melodramatic accounts of the decadent upper class, most notably La casa del ángel (The House of the Angel, 1957), which was screened and awarded at Cannes. The film is based on a novel by Beatriz Guido, co-writer of the screenplay, who would become his wife and regular screenwriter.

information.contentText: Barren Lives was the only Brazilian film to be named by the British Film Institute as one of the 360 essential works for a film archive. This film clearly shows the strong influence of Italian Neorealism on director Nelson Pereira dos Santos's work, and it became one of the best-known films of the movement known as Cinema Novo, which addressed Brazil's social problems.

content_list.content_text: She adapted La mano en la trampa (The Hand in the Trap, 1961) and Piel de verano (Summerskin, 1961) from her own novels. In El ojo de la cerradura (The Eavesdropper, 1966), Leopoldo Torre Nilsson (1924-1978) took on South American politics more directly, telling the story of a right-wing revolutionary. In the early 1960s, Torre Nilsson's success helped create an Argentine New Wave, partly French-inspired.

quote.quote: Glauber Rocha's Black God, White Devil was the film that never left my mind
quote.author: Bong Joon Ho, director of "Parasite"

content_list.content_text: Among the most notable works of this period are Tres veces Ana (Three Times Ana, 1961), by David José Kohon (1919-2004), which tells three stories of sexuality in which Maria Vaner plays three different women named Ana, and Crónica de un niño solo (Chronicle of a Boy Alone, 1965), by Leonardo Favio (b. 1938), the story of a poor boy in an orphanage.

information.contentText: I Am Cuba is epic Cuban propaganda. María (Luz María Collazo) meets an American at a nightclub and sleeps with him. The stranger leaves, paying for the time she gave him, but also for her crucifix, which he has stolen.

content_list.content_text: However, the most important Argentine film movement of the 1960s was a conscious attempt to move away from foreign models. Fernando Solanas (b. 1936) and Octavio Getino (b. 1935) collaborated on La hora de los hornos: Notas y testimonios sobre el neocolonialismo, la violencia y la liberación (The Hour of the Furnaces, 1968). A didactic account of Argentine history and politics, this film became the model for "Third Cinema": a cinema style of its own for the Third World, an alternative to the "First Cinema" of Hollywood and the "Second Cinema" of the new waves.

The Chilean film industry found its footing in the late 1960s. Avant-garde filmmaker Raúl Ruiz (b. 1941) made his directorial debut with Tres tristes tigres (Three Sad Tigers, 1968), a model of the intellectual games that characterize his work. Most of his career, however, would be spent abroad, mainly in France.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Simon of the Desert
information.contentText: In Luis Buñuel's Simon of the Desert, based on the story of Simeon Stylites, Simon (Claudio Brook) lives atop a column as proof of his faith, which is repeatedly tested.

content_list.content_text: More realistic in style is El Chacal de Nahueltoro (The Jackal of Nahueltoro, 1969), by Miguel Littin (b. 1942), an uneven but extremely vigorous, documentary-style portrait of a murderer whose experiences underpin the dramatization of the desperate living conditions of Chile's poor. After the Marxist Salvador Allende won the 1970 elections, Littin briefly served as president of the state-owned company Chile Films, but resigned before Allende's overthrow forced exile on both him and Ruiz.

None of the other Spanish-speaking countries of South America - Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, Paraguay, and Uruguay - sustained significant film production throughout the 1960s; in some of these countries, only short documentaries were made. However, many of the most notable Latin American films of the decade were produced off the continent, on the Caribbean island of Cuba, where the 1959 revolution had transformed what had until then been a minor industry.

information.contentTitle: Trailer for The Jackal of Nahueltoro
information.contentText: Based on real events, the film recreates a shocking crime that surfaced in Chile's crime news in the mid-1960s, when a peasant named Jorge del Carmen Valenzuela Torres was arrested for the multiple murder of a peasant woman and her five children in the village of Nahueltoro.

content_list.content_text: In 1961, after Cuban leader Fidel Castro nationalized local industries and established ties with the Soviet Union, the United States broke off diplomatic relations, and Castro's regime moved definitively into the Soviet orbit. This new alignment found cinematic expression when Mikhail Kalatozov (1903-1973), the Georgian filmmaker behind the Soviet classic Letyat zhuravli (The Cranes Are Flying, 1957), went to the island to make Soy Cuba (I Am Cuba, 1964). A visually stunning work of propaganda, the film traces the country's path from pre-revolutionary oppression to an idealized, celebratory present.

Cuban filmmaker Tomás Gutiérrez Alea (1928-1996) signed one of the first post-revolutionary productions, the neorealist war film Historias de la revolución (Stories of the Revolution, 1960). His later work contains an evolving dialectical social critique: La muerte de un burócrata (Death of a Bureaucrat, 1966) emerged as a surprising satire of the spasms of socialist bureaucracy, while Memorias del subdesarrollo (Memories of Underdevelopment, 1968), a melancholy account of post-revolutionary life, displays remarkable skeptical intelligence for a film produced under a totalitarian regime.

information.contentTitle: Scene from The Hour of the Furnaces
information.contentText: The Hour of the Furnaces is an exercise in "Third Cinema".

content_list.content_text: That same year, Humberto Solás (1941-2008) made Lucía, a vigorous narrative of women's experience across three different periods of Cuban history, notable for its dramatic intensity and its immaculate period reconstruction.

The circumstances of Cuba, the only Latin American country to carry out a successful and lasting leftist revolution, were unique, but the tendency to make politically engaged films was not, as the open social criticism of the best films made in Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico shows. Latin America in the 1960s was a region where cinema could not afford the luxury of not being political.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: O Pagador de Promessas
movies.overview: Zé do Burro (Leonardo Villar) e sua mulher Rosa (Glória Menezes) vivem em uma pequena propriedade a 42 quilômetros de Salvador. Um dia, o burro de estimação de Zé é atingido por um raio e ele acaba indo a um terreiro de candomblé, onde faz uma promessa a Santa Bárbara para salvar o animal. Com o restabelecimento do bicho, Zé põe-se a cumprir a promessa e doa metade de seu sítio, para depois começar uma caminhada rumo a Salvador, carregando nas costas uma imensa cruz de madeira. Mas a via crucis de Zé ainda se torna mais angustiante ao ver sua mulher se engraçar com o cafetão Bonitão (Geraldo Del Rey) e ao encontrar a resistência ferrenha do padre Olavo (Dionísio Azevedo) a negar-lhe a entrada em sua igreja, pela razão de Zé haver feito sua promessa em um terreiro.

movies.original_title: O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro
movies.title: O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro
movies.overview: Continuação de Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol. Misturando cordel e ópera, esta aventura apresenta o personagem Antônio das Mortes, que recebe a tarefa de eliminar um novo cangaceiro da região. No caminho, ele encontra diversos jagunços e coroneis e se vê cara a cara com o povo do sertão e com as dificuldades enfrentadas pelos sertanejos, eventos que farão Antonio adquirir uma nova perspectiva de vida.

movies.title: A Hora dos Fornos: Notas e Testemunhos do Neocolonialismo, Violência e Libertação
movies.overview: Atual e profético, as preocupações e alertas de Pino Solanas nesta trilogia em 1968 não foram ouvidas e se transformaram nas calamidades que conhecemos durante as décadas seguintes. O conjunto de documentários mostra a História Moderna da América Latina.  Dividido em três partes: 1) “Colonialismo e Violência” 2) “Ato Para a Libertação”, o qual é dividido em dois grandes momentos: Crônica do peronismo (1945-1955) e Crônica da Resistência (1955-1966) 3) “Violência e Libertação”

movies.title: Vidas Secas
movies.overview: Uma família miserável tenta escapar da seca no sertão nordestino. Fabiano (Átila Iório), Sinhá Vitória (Maria Ribeiro), seus dois filhos e a cachorra Baleia vagam sem destino e já quase sem esperanças pelos confins do interior, sobrevivendo às forças da natureza e à crueldade dos homens. Adaptação da obra de Graciliano Ramos.

movies.title: Pele de Verão
movies.overview: Uma jovem aceita fingir que está apaixonada por um rapaz condenado por uma doença mortal, para lhe suavizar o fim da vida. Em troca, tem a promessa de uma luxuosa estadia de um ano em Paris. Mas, no desenlace, há uma surpresa.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1960 to 1969
content_list.description: Brazil catches the world's attention with its Cinema Novo, the sexual revolution of the '60s is reflected in film, psychological horror gains ground, and science fiction, with 2001: A Space Odyssey, wins over audiences and critics. Click here to see, in chronological order, the main events in cinema between 1940 and 1959.
